"Quickly, my children — do as I tell you, so that before all the gods I may win the favor of Athena, who came to me in her own bright presence at the god's rich feast. One of you go to the plain for a heifer, and have the herdsman drive it here at once. Another go down to noble Telemachus' ship and bring up all his crew, leaving only two behind to mind the vessel. And send one to fetch the goldsmith Laerces, to lay the gold around the heifer's horns. The rest of you stay here with me. Tell the women inside to make ready a fine feast through the halls, to set out seats and firewood, and to bring fresh spring water."

So he spoke, and they all hurried to it. The heifer came in from the plain, and the crew came up from Telemachus' swift, balanced ship. The smith came with the tools of his trade in his hands — anvil, hammer, and the well-made tongs he worked his gold with. And Athena herself came, to take her part in the offering. Old Nestor, the knight, gave out the gold, and the smith worked it carefully around the heifer's horns, so the goddess would delight in the sight of it. Stratius and noble Echephron led her forward by the horns. Aretus came from the house carrying water in a flowered basin, with a basket of barley grain in his other hand. Thrasymedes, hardened in war, stood ready with a sharp axe to strike the heifer down, and Perseus held the bowl to catch the blood. Then Nestor, the old knight of Gerene, began the rite — washing his hands, scattering the barley, and praying long to Athena as he cut a tuft from the heifer's head and threw it on the fire.

When they had prayed and flung the barley grain, the son of Nestor, brave Thrasymedes, stepped up and struck. The axe cut clean through the tendons of the neck and the heifer's strength gave way. The women raised their cry — Nestor's daughters and his sons' wives, and his honored wife Eurydice, eldest daughter of Clymenus. Then the men lifted the heifer's head from the wide-wayed earth and held it up, and Pisistratus, leader of men, cut her throat. When the dark blood had run out and the life had left her bones, they cut her up at once. They sliced out the thigh-bones in the proper way, wrapped them in a double layer of fat, and laid raw flesh on top; the old man burned them on split wood and poured bright wine over them, while the young men stood by with five-pronged forks in their hands. When the thigh-bones were burned and they had tasted the inner meats, they carved the rest into small pieces, ran them onto the spits, and roasted them, holding the sharp spits steady over the flame.

Meanwhile Polycaste, Nestor's youngest daughter, lovely as the gods, bathed Telemachus. When she had washed him and rubbed him with olive oil, she dressed him in a fine tunic and cloak, and he stepped from the bath looking like a god, and went to sit beside Nestor, shepherd of the people. When the outer meats were roasted, they drew them off the spits and sat down to the feast, and worthy stewards waited on them, filling their golden cups again and again with wine. And when they had had their fill of food and drink, Nestor, the old knight of Gerene, spoke first: "My sons, bring out the fair-maned horses for Telemachus, and yoke them to the chariot, so he can be on his way."

So he spoke, and they did just as he said, and harnessed the swift horses to the chariot. The housekeeper packed bread and wine and good things to eat, the kind of fare kings' sons live on. Telemachus stepped up into the beautiful chariot, and Nestor's son Pisistratus, a leader of men, took his place beside him and gathered the reins in his hands. He flicked the horses to a start, and they flew off, not unwilling, out into the open country, leaving the high city of Pylos behind. All day long they shook the yoke across their necks, and the sun went down and the roads grew dark. So they came to Pherae, to the house of Diocles, the son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus had fathered. There they spent the night, and Diocles treated them as a host should. And when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, they yoked the horses again and mounted the inlaid chariot, and drove out through the gateway and the echoing portico. Pisistratus flicked the horses on, and they flew, not unwilling — and soon they came to the wheat-bearing plain, and there, near the end of the road, the powerful horses carried them on.

They came down into Lacedaemon, the city in the hollow of the hills, and drove straight to the house of Menelaus. They found him in his halls, hosting a feast for a great gathering of his kinsmen, celebrating two weddings at once — his daughter's and his son's. The daughter he was sending to the son of the warrior Achilles; he had promised her to him long before, while they were still at Troy, and now the gods were bringing the marriage about. So he was sending her off with chariots and horses to the famous city of the Myrmidons, where Achilles' son was king. For his own son he had found a bride out of Sparta, the daughter of Alector. That son, Megapenthes, was the strong child of a slave woman, for the gods gave Helen no more children after she had borne her first, Hermione, a girl as lovely as golden Aphrodite.

So the neighbors and kinsmen of glorious Menelaus were feasting and enjoying themselves under his high roof. A singer sang among them to his lyre, and two acrobats whirled and tumbled through the middle of the hall as he struck up his song.

Telemachus and the son of Nestor reined in their horses at the gate. Eteoneus, a quick servant of Menelaus, came out, saw them, and ran back through the house to bring his lord the news. He went up close and spoke to him with winged words: "Menelaus, cherished by the gods — there are strangers at the door, two men who look like the sons of Zeus himself. Tell me, shall we unyoke their fast horses, or send them on to find welcome somewhere else?"

Fair-haired Menelaus flared with anger. "Eteoneus, son of Boethous — you were never a fool before, but now you're babbling like a child. The two of us ate plenty of other men's bread on the long road home before we got back here, where I pray Zeus may let us rest from sorrow at last. Unyoke the strangers' horses, of course, and bring the men inside to share the feast."

Eteoneus hurried back through the hall and called the other servants to come with him. They led the sweating horses out from under the yoke, tied them at the mangers, and threw down a feed of barley mixed with white grain; they tilted the chariot against the bright wall of the courtyard and brought the men into the splendid house. Telemachus and Pisistratus stared in wonder when they saw it, for a kind of brightness ran through the high halls of glorious Menelaus, like the light of the sun or the moon. When they had filled their eyes with it, they went to the polished baths and washed.

When the maids had bathed them and rubbed them with oil and dressed them in soft cloaks and tunics, they sat down on chairs beside Menelaus. A servant came with water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it over their hands into a silver basin, and drew up a polished table beside them. A grave housekeeper brought bread and laid it out, and many good things besides, giving freely from her stores. A carver lifted platters of every kind of meat and set them down, and placed golden cups beside them.

Then fair-haired Menelaus greeted them, his hand reaching out to them: "Help yourselves, and welcome. When you've had your supper, we'll ask who you are — for a line like yours can't have been lost. You're surely sprung from a family of kings who carry the scepter; common men don't father sons like you."

With that he passed them a fat slice of roast loin from his own portion, the cut of honor set near him, and they reached out for the good things spread before them. When they had taken their fill of food and drink, Telemachus leaned in close to Nestor's son, his head near his so the others wouldn't hear, and said: "Look around, Pisistratus, man after my own heart — the flash of bronze through these echoing halls, of gold and amber, of ivory and silver. The court of Olympian Zeus must look like this. There's wealth past counting here. I'm lost in wonder at it."

But fair-haired Menelaus overheard him, and said: "Dear boys, no mortal man can rival Zeus. His house and everything in it are immortal. Among men, though — well, maybe one man somewhere is as rich as I am, maybe not. I brought it all home over eight long years of wandering and grief, sailing through Cyprus and Phoenicia and Egypt, reaching the Ethiopians, the Sidonians, the Erembians, and Libya, where the lambs grow horns from birth and the ewes bear young three times a year, so that no master or hired man there ever lacks cheese or meat or sweet milk — the flocks give all year round. But while I was gathering this wealth in those far places, my own brother was murdered behind my back, by the treachery of his cursed wife — and so I take no joy in being lord of all of it. Whoever your fathers are, you've surely heard this from them: how much I suffered, and how I lost a whole house, a fine one, full of good things. I'd gladly live with only a third of this wealth, if the men were still alive who died on the wide plain of Troy, far from the grazing land of Argos. I grieve for all of them, sitting here in my halls. Sometimes I ease my heart with weeping, and sometimes I stop — a man tires soon enough of cold tears. But of them all there's one I mourn for most, one whose memory turns me from food and sleep, since no Greek labored as hard or risked as much as Odysseus. For him it was all suffering, and for me a grief that won't heal, he's been gone so long, and we don't even know if he's alive or dead. By now they must be mourning him — old Laertes, and steadfast Penelope, and Telemachus, the boy he left behind, newly born."

So he spoke, and stirred in Telemachus a longing to weep for his father. The tears spilled from his eyes to the ground at the sound of that name, and he lifted his purple cloak in both hands to cover his face. Menelaus saw it, and wavered in his heart — whether to let the young man speak of his father in his own time, or to question him first and draw it out of him.

While he was still turning it over, Helen came down from her high, fragrant, vaulted room, lovely as Artemis of the golden arrows. Adraste set a well-made chair for her, Alcippe spread soft wool across it, and Phylo carried in the silver work-basket given to Helen by Alcandra, the wife of Polybus, who lived in Egyptian Thebes, the richest city on earth. Polybus had given Menelaus two silver bathtubs, two tripods, and ten talents of gold; and his wife gave Helen her own fine gifts — a golden distaff, and this silver basket that ran on little wheels, its rim finished in gold. Phylo set it down beside her now, packed with spun yarn, the distaff laid across it charged with violet wool. Helen sank into the chair, set her feet on the stool, and at once began questioning her husband.

"Do we know, Menelaus, cherished by the gods, who these men say they are, these strangers come to our house? I may be wrong, but my heart won't let me keep silent — I have to say it. I've never seen anyone, man or woman, so like another as this young man is like the son of brave Odysseus. He must be Telemachus, the child Odysseus left as a newborn at home when you Greeks came to Troy with war in your hearts, all for the sake of my own shameless self."

And fair-haired Menelaus answered her: "I see it now too, wife, the likeness you've caught. These are Odysseus' hands and feet, the same set of his head, the same hair, the very eyes. And just now, when I was speaking of Odysseus, of all he endured and suffered for my sake, the bitter tears welled up in this young man's eyes and he hid his face behind his cloak."

Then Pisistratus, Nestor's son, spoke up: "Menelaus, son of Atreus, cherished by the gods — you're right, this is the son of that man. But he's modest, and ashamed, coming here for the first time, to throw himself into talk before you, whose voice we delight in like a god's. My father, the old knight Nestor, sent me along to bring him here, for Telemachus wanted to see you, hoping you might give him some word or counsel. A son has hard troubles at home when his father is gone and no one else stands beside him — and that is just how it is for Telemachus now. His father is far away, and there's no one in the land to keep the wolves from his door."

And fair-haired Menelaus answered: "What a thing — that the son of a man I loved so dearly should come to my house, a man who bore so much hardship for my sake. I always swore that if he came home, I would honor him beyond all the other Greeks — if only Zeus had let the two of us sail back safe across the sea. I'd have given him a city to live in here in Argos, built him a house, brought him from Ithaca with his son and all his goods and people, emptying out one of the towns nearby that look to me as their lord. We'd have lived side by side, dear to each other always, and nothing would have parted us but the black cloud of death. But the god himself must have begrudged us that, for he alone of all men is kept from coming home."

So he spoke, and his words set them all weeping. Helen, child of Zeus, wept; Telemachus wept; and so did Menelaus, son of Atreus. Nor could Nestor's son keep his eyes from filling, for his heart turned to his noble brother Antilochus, cut down by the splendid son of the Dawn. Thinking of him, he spoke to Menelaus with winged words: "Son of Atreus — my father Nestor always called you the wisest of men, whenever we spoke of you in his halls. So, if you can, do as I ask. I take no pleasure in weeping over supper, and besides, the Dawn will rise soon enough — there is no harm, then, in mourning whoever has died and met his fate. This is the only honor we can pay the wretched dead: to cut our hair for them and let the tears run down our cheeks. I lost a brother too, a far from worthless man — you surely knew him. His name was Antilochus, and they say no one was faster on his feet or braver in a fight. I never saw him myself."

And fair-haired Menelaus answered him: "My friend, you've spoken with more sense than your years should allow — clearly the son of a wise father. You can always tell the breeding of a man whose line Zeus has blessed in his marriage and his children, the way he has blessed Nestor, all his days, with a smooth old age in his own halls and sons about him both wise and good with a spear. So let's leave off the weeping that broke over us, and turn back to our supper — and have them pour water over our hands. There'll be time enough in the morning for Telemachus and me to talk it all through."
So Asphalion, one of the quick servants of glorious Menelaus, poured water over their hands, and they reached out again for the good things spread before them.

Then Helen, child of Zeus, thought of something else. Into the wine they were drinking she slipped a drug that quiets all pain and anger and brings forgetfulness of every sorrow. Whoever drank it down, once it was mixed in the bowl, could not let a single tear fall the whole day long, not even if his own mother and father lay dead, not even if armed men cut down his brother or his beloved son right before his eyes, and he watched it happen. Helen had been given this drug, so cunning and so potent, by Polydamna, the wife of Thon, a woman of Egypt — where the rich earth grows herbs past counting, some healing, some deadly when mixed, and every man is a healer skilled beyond all others, for they are the kin of Paeon, the gods' own physician. When she had stirred the drug in and ordered the wine poured round, Helen spoke again:

"Menelaus, son of Atreus, cherished by the gods — and you young men, sons of good fathers — the god gives us now this thing and now that, for Zeus can do anything, and to one man he sends good and to another evil. So feast at your ease in the hall and take pleasure in the talk; I'll tell you a story that suits the hour. I couldn't name every labor of long-suffering Odysseus, but I'll tell you one — what that bold man dared and brought off in the land of the Trojans, where you Greeks were grinding through such hardship. He laid degrading welts across his own body, threw filthy rags over his shoulders like a slave, and slipped into the enemy's wide streets disguised as a beggar, nothing like the man he was among the Greek ships. In that disguise he went into Troy, and not one of them suspected him — I alone knew him for who he was, and questioned him, but he was too sly and kept slipping away. Only after I had bathed him and rubbed him with oil and dressed him and sworn a great oath never to give him up to the Trojans until he was safely back at the ships did he tell me the whole plan of the Greeks. Then he cut down a good many Trojans with his long sword and got away to the Greek camp, carrying everything he had learned. The Trojan women wailed aloud — but my own heart sang, for by then it had turned toward home, and I grieved over the madness Aphrodite laid on me when she carried me there, far from my own dear land, my child, my marriage, and a husband who lacked nothing, in looks or in wit."

And fair-haired Menelaus answered her: "Yes, wife, everything you've said is true. I have known the minds and the counsels of many heroes, and traveled over much of the world, but never with my own eyes have I seen a heart like the heart of long-suffering Odysseus. Think what that strong man dared and endured inside the wooden horse, where the best of the Greeks sat waiting in the dark to bring slaughter and doom on the Trojans. You came to us there — some god who wanted the Trojans to win must have sent you, and godlike Deiphobus came at your side. Three times you circled the hollow trap, running your hands along it, calling out the names of the Greek captains one by one, mimicking the voices of all their wives. I was sitting in the middle with Diomedes and brilliant Odysseus, and we heard you crying out. The two of us half rose, burning either to rush out or to answer you from inside — but Odysseus held us back and stopped us, for all our longing. Every other Greek there sat dead still, except Anticlus, who started to call back to you. But Odysseus clamped his two strong hands hard over the man's mouth and held them there, and so he saved us all, keeping his grip until Athena drew you away again."

Then thoughtful Telemachus said to him: "Menelaus, son of Atreus, cherished by the gods — it only makes the grief worse, that none of this saved him from a wretched end, for all his iron heart. But now send us to bed, I beg you, so we may lie down and take the sweet gift of sleep."

So he spoke, and Helen of Argos told her maids to set up beds under the colonnade, to pile them with fine purple rugs, to spread coverlets on top and lay out thick woolen cloaks. The maids went out from the hall with torches in their hands and made up the beds, and a herald led the guests away. So Telemachus and the splendid son of Nestor slept there in the forecourt of the house, while the son of Atreus lay deep within the high hall, and beside him lay Helen in her long robe, loveliest of women.

When rosy-fingered Dawn, child of morning, appeared, Menelaus, lord of the great war-cry, rose from his bed and dressed. He slung his sharp sword over his shoulder, bound fine sandals beneath his shining feet, and came from his room like a god to look on. He took a seat beside Telemachus, and asked: "Tell me, Telemachus — what need has brought you all this way over the sea's broad back to Lacedaemon? Is it some matter of your people, or your own? Tell me the truth."

And thoughtful Telemachus answered him: "Menelaus, son of Atreus, cherished by the gods — I came in the hope you might tell me something of my father. My house is being eaten alive, my rich fields laid waste; the place is crammed with hostile men who keep slaughtering my flocks and my shambling, twist-horned cattle, all while courting my mother in their arrogance. So I come and clasp your knees, in the hope you'll tell me how he met his bitter end — whether you saw it with your own eyes, or heard it from some other wanderer. His mother bore him for grief. Don't soften it out of pity for me. Tell me plainly, just as you saw it. If my brave father Odysseus ever served you well, by word or deed, in the years you Greeks suffered at Troy, remember it now, and tell me everything, exactly true."

Then fair-haired Menelaus answered him, deeply stirred: "Shameless cowards — to think they'd lie down in the bed of a man like that! It's as if a deer had laid her newborn fawns to sleep in a lion's den and gone off to graze the wooded glens, and the lion came home to his lair and tore them apart, both of them, in a moment — that's how Odysseus will deal with those men, and bring their ugly fate on them. Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo — if only the Odysseus who once stood up in lovely Lesbos and wrestled the son of Philomeleides and threw him down so hard that all the Greeks cheered — if only that Odysseus could meet these suitors now. They'd find their lives cut short and their marriage turned bitter. But as for what you ask me and beg me to tell — I won't twist it aside or deceive you. Of all the old sea-god told me, I'll hide nothing.

"The gods kept me penned in Egypt, hungry to come home, because I hadn't given them their full offering of sacred hecatombs, and the gods always want their dues remembered. There's an island out in the surging sea, off the mouth of Egypt — Pharos they call it, about as far offshore as a hollow ship can run in a day with a stiff wind astern. It has a good harbor where men can draw fresh water and launch their trim ships back to sea. There the gods becalmed me twenty days; not once did the steady winds rise off the water that carry a ship across the sea's wide back. All our food would have given out, and the men's strength with it, if a goddess hadn't pitied me and saved me — Eidothea, daughter of mighty Proteus, the old man of the sea. I had touched her heart most of all.

"She came to me one day when I was off alone, away from my men, who were forever roaming the island with their barbed hooks, fishing — for hunger was wearing at their bellies. She stood close and said: 'Stranger, are you such a fool, so slack of heart, or do you let things slide on purpose, and even enjoy your own suffering? You've been trapped on this island so long now, and can't find any way off it, while the spirit of your men drains out of them.'

"And I answered her: 'I'll tell you, whichever of the goddesses you are — I'm not stuck here by any choice of mine. I must have sinned against the deathless gods who hold the wide heaven. So tell me — you gods know everything — which of the immortals is binding me here and blocking my way, and how I'm to sail home over the teeming sea.'

"And the bright goddess answered: 'Then I'll tell you, stranger, and tell you straight. An old immortal of the sea comes haunting these waters — Proteus of Egypt, who never lies, who knows the depths of every sea, the servant of Poseidon. They say he is my father, that he sired me. If you could somehow lay an ambush and catch him, he would tell you your course, the stages of your voyage, and how to sail home over the teeming sea. And if you wished it, son of Zeus, he would tell you all that has happened in your halls, good and bad, while you have wandered so long and so hard a road.'
"And I said: 'Then show me yourself the way to ambush this old god, before he sees me coming and slips away. A god is hard for a mortal man to master.'

"And the bright goddess answered at once: 'I'll tell you, stranger, and tell you straight. When the sun has climbed to the middle of the sky, the truthful old man of the sea comes up out of the water, under the breath of the West Wind, hidden by the dark ripple it raises over him. Once he's out, he lies down to sleep in the hollow of the caves, and around him the seals, the brood of the lovely salt-sea goddess, haul up out of the grey water and sleep in herds, breathing up the sharp stink of the sea's deep places. Tomorrow at first light I'll lead you there and lay you down in a row. Choose your three best men, the bravest in your ships. And I'll tell you all the old man's tricks.

"'First he'll go down the line of his seals and count them. When he has them all tallied off on his fingers, he'll lie down among them like a shepherd among his flock. The moment you see him stretched out asleep, throw everything you have into holding him fast, hard as he fights to break free. He'll try to turn into every creature that crawls the earth, and into water too, and into blazing fire. But hold him without flinching, and grip him harder still. Then, when at last he speaks to you and asks his questions in the same shape he wore when you saw him sleeping, let go your hold, hero, and free the old man — and ask him which of the gods is set against you, and how you're to sail home over the teeming sea.'

"With that she dove under the swell of the sea, and I went back to my ships drawn up on the sand, my heart dark with care as I walked. When I reached the ships and the water, we made our supper, and the holy night came down, and we lay to sleep on the breaking shore. When rosy-fingered Dawn, child of morning, appeared, I went out along the shore of the wide sea, praying hard to the gods, with the three men I trusted most for any work. Meanwhile the goddess had dived deep into the sea's broad lap and brought up four sealskins, all freshly flayed — she was laying a trap for her own father. She scooped out four beds in the sand and sat waiting for us. When we came up she had us lie down side by side, and threw a skin over each of us. That ambush would have been unbearable — the deadly rank stench of the sea-bred seals choked us; who would lie down beside a monster of the deep? But the goddess saved us; she thought of a great relief and dabbed ambrosia under each man's nose, sweet-smelling, and it killed the seals' reek.

"All morning we waited, holding ourselves steady, and the seals came up from the sea in herds and stretched out along the breaking shore. At noon the old man came up out of the sea, found his fat seals, and went down the whole line counting them. We were the first he counted off, among his beasts, never dreaming there was any trick — and then he lay down himself. With a great shout we rushed him, and threw our arms around him, and the old man never forgot his cunning craft: first he turned into a great bearded lion, then a serpent, a leopard, a huge boar; he turned into running water, and into a tall leafy tree. But we held on, gripping him, our hearts unshaken, until at last the old wizard, worn out, broke and spoke to me: 'Which of the gods, son of Atreus, plotted with you to trap me against my will and seize me? What is it you want?'

"And I answered him: 'You know, old man — why feint and ask? You know I've been penned on this island so long, and I can find no way off, and the heart in me is failing. So tell me — you gods know everything — which of the immortals is binding me here and blocking my way, and how I'm to sail home over the teeming sea.'

"And he answered me at once: 'Why, you should have made fine offerings to Zeus and the other gods before you sailed, if you wanted the quickest crossing home over the wine-dark sea. For it is not your fate to see your own people and reach your fine house and your native land until you have gone back once more to the waters of Egypt, the rain-fed river, and offered the holy gods who hold the wide heaven their sacred hecatombs. Only then will the gods grant you the road you long for.'

"So he spoke, and the heart broke in me, that he should send me back over the misty sea to Egypt, that long and weary way. Still, I answered him: 'I'll do it all, old man, just as you command. But tell me this, and tell me true: did all the Greeks come home safe in their ships, all the ones Nestor and I left behind when we sailed from Troy? Or did any die a hard death aboard his own ship, or in the arms of his friends, once the fighting was done?'

"And he answered me at once: 'Son of Atreus, why ask me this? You're better off not knowing what I know, for once you've heard, I don't think your eyes will stay dry. Many of them are dead, and many came through. Of the captains, only two of the bronze-clad Greeks died on the way home — you were there yourself for the fighting — and a third is still alive, held somewhere on the broad sea. Ajax went down among his long-oared ships. Poseidon first drove him onto the great rocks of Gyrae, but pulled him clear of the water, and he'd have escaped his doom, hated as he was by Athena, if he hadn't let one wild, reckless boast slip out: that he'd come through the sea's depths in spite of the gods. Poseidon heard that great talk, and took his trident in his strong hands and struck the rock of Gyrae and split it. One half held; but the broken piece, the one Ajax had been sitting on when he made his mad boast, plunged into the sea and carried him down with it, into the surging deep, and he drank the salt water and died.

"'Your brother slipped past the death-spirits in his hollow ships — Hera saved him. But just as he was about to round the steep height of Malea, a storm caught him and carried him groaning out across the teeming sea to the borderland where Thyestes had once lived, and where Aigisthos, his son, was living now. Even from there a safe homecoming opened before him; the gods turned the wind around, and they reached home, and Agamemnon stepped out onto his own soil with joy, and bent and kissed the earth of his fatherland, and the warm tears streamed down at the sight of the land he loved.

"'But a watchman saw him from his lookout — a man Aigisthos had set there, promising him two talents of gold. He'd been watching a whole year so that Agamemnon couldn't pass unseen and seize the first blow. He ran to the house with the news, and Aigisthos at once set his treacherous trap. He picked twenty of his best men and hid them in ambush, and on the far side of the hall he had a feast laid out. Then he went with chariots and horses to fetch Agamemnon, his mind full of murder, and led him home all unsuspecting, and cut him down at the feast the way a man kills an ox at the manger. Not one of the men who came with the son of Atreus was left alive, and not one of Aigisthos' men — they all died there in the hall.'

"So Proteus spoke, and the heart broke in me. I sank down on the sand and wept; I had no wish to go on living or to see the light of the sun. But when I had wept and writhed in the sand till I had my fill, the old man of the sea said: 'Son of Atreus, don't keep on weeping like this, so long and so hard — it does no good. Get yourself back to your own land as fast as you can. You may yet find the man alive — or Orestes may have killed him first, and you'll come in time for the funeral feast.'

"So he spoke, and for all my grief, the heart in my breast warmed again. I said to him with winged words: 'These two I know of now. Tell me the third — the man you said was still alive, held somewhere on the broad sea. Or is he dead? Tell me, even if it brings me grief.'

"And he answered me at once: 'The third is Odysseus, son of Laertes, whose home is in Ithaca. I saw him on an island, weeping hard, in the halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him there against his will, so that he can't reach his own land; he has no oared ships and no crew to carry him over the sea's broad back. As for you, Menelaus, cherished by the gods — it is not your fate to die in horse-pasturing Argos and meet your end there. The immortals will send you to the Elysian Fields, the world's end, where fair-haired Rhadamanthus lives and life is easiest for men: no snow there, no heavy storm, no rain ever, but the Ocean sends up a singing West Wind, always, to bring its coolness to men. This will be yours because you married Helen, and so are the son-in-law of Zeus.'

"With that he dove back under the swell of the sea, and I went to my ships with my godlike men, my heart dark with care as I walked. When we reached the ships and the water, we made our supper, and the holy night came down, and we lay to sleep on the breaking shore. When rosy-fingered Dawn, child of morning, appeared, we hauled the ships down into the bright sea and set the masts and sails into the trim hulls, and the men climbed aboard and took their places at the oars and beat the grey sea white. So I brought the ships back once more to the rain-fed waters of Egypt, and there I offered full and faultless hecatombs. And when I had soothed the anger of the everlasting gods, I raised a barrow to Agamemnon, so his name would never die. Then I set sail, and the gods gave me a fair wind and brought me swiftly home, back to my own dear land.

"But now stay here in my halls eleven or twelve more days, and then I'll send you off in style. I'll give you splendid gifts — three horses and a polished chariot — and a beautiful cup as well, so that all your days, whenever you pour an offering to the immortal gods, you'll remember me."

And thoughtful Telemachus answered him: "Son of Atreus, don't keep me here too long. I'd gladly sit beside you a whole year and never once feel the pull of home or my parents — your stories and your talk are such a delight to me. But by now my crew, waiting in sacred Pylos, must be wearing thin, and you're holding me here too long. As for the gift you'd press on me — let it be something I can store away. I won't take horses back to Ithaca; better to leave them here, an ornament for your own stables. You rule a wide flat plain, thick with clover and galingale, with wheat and broad-eared white barley. But Ithaca has no broad running-ground, no meadow at all. It's a land for goats, and dearer to me for that than any land for grazing horses. None of the islands that lean down to the sea is good for driving horses or rich in meadow, and Ithaca least of all."

So he spoke, and Menelaus, lord of the great war-cry, smiled, and stroked the young man's hand, and said: "Good blood shows in your talk, dear boy. Yes — I'll change the gift; that's easy enough. Of all the treasures stored in my house I'll give you the loveliest and most precious of them all: a mixing bowl, finely wrought, of solid silver, its rim finished in gold, the work of Hephaestus himself. Phaedimus, king of the Sidonians, gave it to me when his house took me in on my way home. That is what I want to give you."

So the two of them talked on, while guests kept arriving at the great king's house. They drove up sheep, and brought wine to lift the heart, and their veiled wives sent along the bread. So they busied themselves over the feast in the halls of Menelaus.

But back in Ithaca, the suitors were amusing themselves with throwing the discus and the hunting spear on the leveled ground before Odysseus' house, swaggering as always. Antinous and godlike Eurymachus were sitting apart, the ringleaders, the best of them by far. Noemon, son of Phronius, came up to them and asked Antinous: "Antinous, do we have any idea when Telemachus is coming back from sandy Pylos? He's gone off with a ship of mine, and I need it now — to cross to the wide pastures of Elis, where I have twelve brood mares with sturdy mule foals at the teat, still unbroken. I want to drive one home and break him in."

He spoke, and they were stunned; they'd never imagined Telemachus had gone to Pylos, the city of Neleus. They'd thought he was somewhere on the land nearby, out with the flocks, or with the swineherd. So Antinous, son of Eupeithes, said to him: "Tell me the truth — when did he go, and what young men went with him? Picked men of Ithaca, or his own hired hands and slaves? He could have managed that too. And tell me this straight: did he take your black ship by force, against your will, or did you give it freely when he asked?"

And Noemon, son of Phronius, answered him: "I gave it freely myself. What else could anyone do, when a man like that, with such a weight on him, asks a favor? It would have been hard to refuse. And the young men who sailed with him are the best in the land, after ourselves. I saw Mentor go aboard as their captain — or a god who looked exactly like him. But that's the strange thing: I saw godlike Mentor here, in town, only yesterday at dawn — and yet by then he had already boarded the ship for Pylos."

With that Noemon went off to his father's house, and the proud hearts of the other two were stung. They called the suitors in from their games and sat them down, and Antinous, son of Eupeithes, rose to speak, sick with rage, his dark heart swollen and his eyes like blazing fire: "This is a bad business — Telemachus has carried off this voyage in style, and we swore it would come to nothing. The boy has slipped away in spite of us all, with a launched ship and a picked crew. He'll be more trouble yet. But may Zeus break his strength before he reaches his full growth. Give me a fast ship and twenty men, and I'll lie in wait for him in the strait between Ithaca and rocky Same, and ambush him as he comes — and bitter will be this voyage he made, hunting for word of his father."
So he spoke, and they all cheered him on and urged him to it; then they rose and went into the house of Odysseus.

But Penelope did not stay long in the dark about what the suitors were plotting in their hearts. The herald Medon told her — he had overheard their schemes from the courtyard while they laid their plans inside. He went through the house to bring the word to Penelope, and as he crossed her threshold she said to him: "Herald, why have the proud suitors sent you here? To tell the serving women of godlike Odysseus to leave their work and cook a feast for them? I wish they would never woo, never gather again — that this very meal might be their last. You crowd in here day after day, eating up the living of wise Telemachus. Did your own fathers never tell you, when you were children, what kind of man Odysseus was among them? He never wronged a soul, by word or deed, in all the land — though that is the way of kings, to love one man and hate another. Never once did he do a brutal thing to any man. But your black hearts and your ugly deeds are plain to see — and there's no gratitude left for kindness done."

Then Medon, the wise herald, answered her: "My queen, I only wish that were the worst of it. But they're plotting something far more terrible now — may the son of Kronos never let it happen. They mean to kill Telemachus with the sharp bronze as he sails home. He has gone for news of his father, to sacred Pylos and to splendid Lacedaemon."

So he spoke, and her knees gave way and the heart melted in her breast. For a long while she could not say a word; her eyes filled with tears, and her full voice was stopped. At last she found speech and said: "Herald — why has my son gone? There was no need for him to board the swift ships that men ride like horses across the great water's salt expanse. Does he want even his name wiped out among men?"

Then Medon, the wise herald, answered her: "I don't know whether some god set him on, or whether his own heart drove him to go to Pylos, to learn whether his father is coming home, or what fate he has met." With that he went back through the house of Odysseus.

And a cloud of heart-wasting grief came over Penelope. She could not bring herself to sit on any of the many chairs in the room; she sank down on the threshold of her richly made chamber and wept, a thin, piteous sound, while all the serving women in the house, young and old, mourned around her. Through her sobbing Penelope said to them: "Listen, my dears — the gods have given me more sorrow than any woman born and raised beside me. First I lost my brave husband, the lion-hearted man, finest in every excellence among the Greeks, whose name was great through Hellas and the heart of Argos. And now the storm-winds have snatched away my own dear son, with no glory and no warning, out of these halls — and I never even heard him go. Hard-hearted, all of you — not one of you thought to rouse me from my bed, though you knew it in your hearts, the very hour he went down to board the hollow black ship. If I had known he meant this journey, he'd have stayed, however set he was on going — or left me dead behind him in these halls. But go, someone, and call old Dolius quickly, the servant my father gave me when I first came here, who keeps my orchard of trees. Have him run to Laertes, sit beside him, and tell him everything, in case Laertes can weave some plan in his mind and come out to plead with the people — these men so bent on wiping out his line and the line of godlike Odysseus."

Then the dear old nurse Eurykleia answered her: "Dear child — kill me with the pitiless bronze if you like, or let me live in the house, but I won't keep the truth from you. I knew all of it. I gave him everything he asked, bread and sweet wine, and he made me swear a great oath not to tell you for ten or twelve days, unless you missed him yourself or heard that he'd gone, so the tears wouldn't spoil your lovely face. But wash now, and put on clean clothes, and go up to your room with your women and pray to Athena, daughter of Zeus who holds the storm-shield — she can save him even from death. And don't trouble the old man; he has burdens enough. I can't believe the blessed gods so hate the line of Arceisius. Someone of it will live on yet, to hold the high-roofed halls and the rich fields stretching far around."

So she spoke, and stilled Penelope's grief and dried the tears from her eyes. Penelope washed, and put on clean clothes, and climbed to the upper room with her women. She set barley grains in a basket and prayed to Athena: "Hear me, child of Zeus who holds the storm-shield, you who never tire. If ever wise Odysseus burned the rich thigh-pieces of ox or sheep to you in these halls, remember it now, and save my dear son, and keep these arrogant suitors far from him."

She cried out as she prayed, and the goddess heard her. But down in the shadowy halls the suitors were in an uproar, and one of those insolent young men was saying: "There's no doubt the queen, courted by us all, is getting ready for her wedding — and never a thought that her son's death has been decided." So he spoke, in his ignorance of how things stood. Then Antinous spoke up among them: "You fools — give up this big, reckless talk, every one of you, or someone may carry it inside. Come, let's get up and quietly carry out the plan we've all agreed on."

With that he chose twenty of the best men, and they went down to the swift ship and the shore of the sea. First they dragged the black ship into deep water, then set up the mast and sails in her, lashed the oars in their leather loops in good order, and ran the white sails up. Their proud servants brought down their armor. They anchored her well out in the water, then went ashore and took their supper, waiting for evening to fall.

But upstairs in her room steadfast Penelope lay, tasting no food, touching neither meat nor drink, wondering only whether her blameless son would slip the death they planned or be brought down by the arrogant suitors. Like a lion ringed by a closing crowd of hunters, sick with dread, she turned it over and over in her mind, until sweet sleep came over her and she sank back, every joint loosened, and slept.

Then grey-eyed Athena thought of something else. She made a phantom, shaping it like a woman — like Iphthime, the daughter of great-hearted Icarius, Penelope's own sister, who had married Eumelus and lived in Pherae. Athena sent the phantom to the house of godlike Odysseus, to ease Penelope of her sobbing and her tears. It slipped into her room past the strap that drew the bolt, and stood above her head and spoke: "You're asleep, Penelope, your heart worn out with grieving. But the gods who live at ease will not let you weep and suffer so. Your son will come home yet, for he has done the gods no wrong."

And steadfast Penelope answered her, drowsing sweetly at the gates of dreams: "Why have you come, sister? You've never come before — you live so very far away. And you tell me to leave off grieving, to quiet all the pains that crowd my heart and mind — I, who have lost my brave, lion-hearted husband, finest in every excellence among the Greeks, whose name was great through Hellas and the heart of Argos? And now my own dear son has gone off in a hollow ship, a boy who knows nothing of hard work or the councils of men. I grieve for him even more than for his father. I tremble for him, afraid of what may happen — whether harm will come to him among the people he's gone to, or out on the sea. He has many enemies, and they plot against him, hungry to kill him before he reaches his own land."

Then the dim phantom answered her: "Take heart, and don't let your mind be so torn with fear. There is one going with him such as other men would pray to have at their side, for she has the power — Pallas Athena. She pities you in your grief, and it is she who has sent me to tell you this."

And steadfast Penelope said to her: "If you are a god, and have heard the voice of a god, then tell me of that other unhappy man as well — is he still alive somewhere, and sees the light of the sun? Or is he dead by now, and down in the house of Hades?"

Then the dim phantom answered her: "I will not tell you the whole of it, whether he's alive or dead. It's no good speaking words as empty as the wind." And with that it slipped out past the bolt of the door and melted into the moving air. But Penelope, daughter of Icarius, started up out of her sleep, and the heart in her was warmed — so clear had the dream come to her in the dead of night.

Meanwhile the suitors had boarded and were sailing the sea-roads, their hearts set on Telemachus' sudden death. Out in the open water, midway between Ithaca and rocky Same, there's a small rocky island, Asteris, with twin harbors where a ship can shelter. There the Greeks lay in wait for him.

Now Dawn rose from her bed beside Tithonus, to bring her light to gods and mortals alike, and the gods sat down in council, and among them Zeus the lord of thunder, who is mightiest of all. And Athena began to tell them of the many troubles of Odysseus, for it weighed on her that he was still in the nymph Calypso's house.

"Father Zeus," she said, "and all you other blessed gods who live forever — let no sceptered king ever again be kind, or gentle, or fair-minded. Let every one of them be cruel from now on, and rule by force. For not a single soul among the people Odysseus once ruled remembers him now — and he ruled them as gently as a father. There he lies, suffering terribly on an island, in the halls of the nymph Calypso, who keeps him against his will. He has no way home — no ships, no crew to carry him over the wide back of the sea. And now they mean to kill his only son as well, when he comes home, for the boy has gone to sandy Pylos and to Sparta, to ask after his father."

"My child," Zeus the cloud-gatherer answered her, "what a thing to let past your lips. Wasn't this your own plan — that Odysseus should come home and pay these men back? And as for Telemachus, you can see him safely home yourself; you have the power. Bring the boy back to his own land untouched, and let the suitors come sailing home empty-handed, their murder undone."

Then he turned to his dear son Hermes. "Hermes — you are our messenger in all things — go to the lovely-haired nymph and tell her our firm decision: that long-suffering Odysseus is to go home. He goes with no escort, neither of gods nor men. On a raft of bound timbers he is to suffer for twenty days and reach Scheria, the rich land of the Phaeacians, who are close kin to the gods. They will honor him like one of the immortals and send him on by ship to his own country, with more bronze and gold and fine cloth than he would ever have carried home from Troy, had he come back unharmed with his full share of the spoils. For it is his fate to see his own people again, and stand once more in his high-roofed house, in the land of his fathers."

So he spoke, and Hermes the runner, the slayer of Argos, did not disobey. At once he bound beneath his feet the beautiful sandals, immortal and golden, that carry him over the water and the endless earth as fast as the wind. And he took up the wand he uses to charm men's eyes shut, or to wake the sleeping when he pleases. With it in his hand he flew, swooping down past Pieria from the high air to the sea, and skimmed the waves like a gull that hunts the fish in the deep folds of the restless water and wets its thick wings in the spray. On and on he went over the endless swell, until he came to that far-off island. There he stepped from the violet sea onto dry land and walked until he reached the great cave where the lovely-haired nymph made her home. And he found her there.

A great fire was burning on the hearth, and the sweet smell of split cedar and juniper drifted far across the island as it burned. Inside, Calypso was singing in a beautiful voice, working her loom, driving the golden shuttle back and forth. Around the cave a wood had grown up thick and green — alder, black poplar, and sweet-smelling cypress, where long-winged birds roosted: owls and hawks and the chattering sea-crows that do their business out on the water. A garden vine, heavy with grapes, ran trailing around the mouth of the cave, and four springs in a row poured out their clear water, each one channeled off in a different direction, and all around soft meadows of violet and wild parsley were in bloom. Even a god, coming upon that place, would stop and marvel, and feel the heart lift within him. And so Hermes, the keen-eyed slayer of Argos, stood and gazed his fill — and then went inside.

Calypso, fair among goddesses, knew him the moment she saw his face, for the gods all know one another, no matter how far apart they live. But she did not find brilliant Odysseus within; he was sitting out on the shore, as always, breaking his heart with tears and groans, staring through his weeping eyes at the barren sea. She gave Hermes a bright, shining chair and asked him: "Hermes — honored friend, and always welcome, though you come to me so seldom — why have you come now? Tell me what's on your mind. My heart says do it, if I can, and if it can be done at all. But first come in, and let me set something before you."

With that the goddess drew up a table laden with ambrosia and mixed him the red nectar, and the slayer of Argos ate and drank his fill. Then, when he had supped, he answered her. "You ask me, goddess to god, why I have come, and I will tell you straight, since you ask it. Zeus ordered me here; it was none of my own doing. Who would choose to cross all this endless salt water, where there is no city of men to offer the gods their sacrifices and choice hundred-beasts? But no god can slip past the will of Zeus who carries the storm-shield, or set it aside. He says you have here the unluckiest of all the men who fought nine years around King Priam's city and sailed home in the tenth, after they had sacked it. On the way home they wronged Athena, and she raised wind and high seas against them, so that all his brave companions were lost, and he alone was carried here by wind and wave. Zeus commands you to send this man on his way at once. It is not his fate to die here, far from his own people. He is to see them again, and stand in his high-roofed house in the land of his fathers."

Calypso, fair among goddesses, shuddered with rage at his words. "You are cruel, you gods," she cried, "and grudging beyond all others. You cannot bear to see a goddess take a mortal man to her bed and live with him openly as her husband. So it was when rosy-fingered Dawn took Orion for herself — you gods who live in ease could not rest until chaste Artemis came to Ortygia and shot him down with her gentle arrows. And so again when fair-haired Demeter gave in to her heart and lay with Iasion in a thrice-plowed fallow field — Zeus heard of it soon enough and struck the man dead with his blazing bolt. And now you grudge me this — that I keep a mortal man here. I saved him myself, when he came drifting astride a single keel, all alone, after Zeus had split his fast ship with a bright bolt and shattered it in the middle of the wine-dark sea. All his brave companions drowned; he alone was carried here by wind and wave. I took him in. I loved him, and cared for him, and meant to make him deathless, never to grow old, all his days. But no god can slip past the will of Zeus who carries the storm-shield, or set it aside. So let him go, if that is what Zeus demands — out over the barren sea. But I cannot send him off myself; I have no ships, no crew to carry him over the water. Still, I will gladly give him what counsel I can, and hide nothing, so he comes home to his own land unharmed."

Then the runner, the slayer of Argos, answered: "Send him off, then, and now — and beware the wrath of Zeus, or he will turn on you one day in anger." And with that the mighty slayer of Argos was gone.

And the queenly nymph went looking for great-hearted Odysseus, now that she had heard the word of Zeus. She found him sitting on the shore, his eyes never dry, his sweet life draining away as he mourned for home — for the nymph no longer pleased him. By night, true, he still slept beside her in the hollow cave, willing no longer, lying beside a goddess who willed it. But by day he sat out on the rocks and the sand, breaking his heart with tears and groans and grief, staring through his weeping eyes at the barren sea. The goddess came close and spoke to him. "My poor man, you needn't sit here grieving any longer, wasting your life away. I am letting you go now, of my own free will. So come — take a bronze axe, cut long timbers, and build yourself a broad raft. Fit an upper deck on it, high enough to carry you safe across the misty sea. And I will stock it with bread and water and red wine to keep the hunger off, and put clothes on your back, and send a fair wind behind you, so you reach your own land unharmed — if that is the will of the gods who hold the wide heaven, who are stronger than I am, and know these things better."

Long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus shuddered as he heard her, and his words came winged: "Goddess, you're plotting something here — this is no help home. You tell me to cross the great gulf of the sea, that hard and terrible water, on a raft — when not even a trim, fast ship runs that course gladly, even with a fair wind from Zeus. No. I will not set foot on a raft unless you bring yourself to swear me a great oath, goddess, that you are scheming no fresh harm against me."

Calypso, fair among goddesses, smiled at that and stroked him with her hand, and said his name. "You are a rogue, and no fool, to think of asking such a thing. Then let the earth be my witness, and the wide heaven above, and the down-flowing water of the Styx — which is the greatest, most dreadful oath the blessed gods can swear — that I am scheming no fresh harm against you. No, I have in mind for you only what I would plan for myself, if ever I came to such straits. My own heart is fair-minded; it is not made of iron. There is pity in me."

With that the queenly goddess led the way, quickly, and the man followed in the god's footsteps. They came to the hollow cave, the goddess and the man, and he sat down on the chair that Hermes had risen from, and the nymph set out before him all kinds of food, the things that mortal men eat and drink. She took her own seat facing godlike Odysseus, and her handmaids set ambrosia and nectar before her, and the two of them reached out and helped themselves to the good things laid ready. And when they had taken their fill of food and drink, Calypso, fair among goddesses, began. "Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many schemes — so you mean to go home, to your own dear country, this very moment? Go, then, and good luck to you. But if you only knew, in your heart, how much suffering you are fated to endure before you reach that land, you would stay here with me and keep this house, and be deathless — for all your longing to see your wife again, the one you ache for, day after day. And yet I think I am no worse than she is — not in form, not in stature. It would hardly be fitting for a mortal woman to match an immortal in body or in beauty."

And Odysseus of the many schemes answered her: "Lady goddess, don't hold this against me. I know it well myself — wise Penelope is nothing beside you to look at, in stature or in beauty. She is mortal, and you are deathless, and never grow old. Even so, all my longing, all my days, is to go home and see the day of my return. And if some god should wreck me out on the wine-dark sea, I will bear it. The heart in my breast is hardened to suffering — I have endured so much already, so much hard labor on the waves and in the war. Let this come too, with the rest."
So he spoke, and the sun went down, and the dark came on, and the two of them went back into the deep of the hollow cave and took their pleasure of love, side by side.

When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, Odysseus pulled on his tunic and his cloak, and the nymph wrapped herself in a long silver robe, fine-woven and graceful, and clasped a beautiful golden belt about her waist, and drew a veil over her head. Then she turned her mind to speeding great-hearted Odysseus on his way. She gave him a great axe that fit his grip, the bronze keen on both edges, with a fine handle of olive-wood set firmly in it; and a smooth-finished adze besides. Then she led him to the far end of the island, where the tall trees grew — alder, black poplar, and fir that reached the sky, long dead and dry, and seasoned, so they would ride light on the water. When she had shown him where the tall trees stood, Calypso, fair among goddesses, went home, and he set to cutting timber, and the work went fast. He felled twenty trees in all and dressed them with the bronze, planed them skillfully, and trued the edges to a chalk-line. Then the goddess brought him augers, and he bored the timbers through and fitted them to one another, and joined them tight with pegs and lashings. As wide as a shipwright skilled in his craft will lay out the hull of a broad cargo ship, so wide did Odysseus build his broad raft. He fixed the deck on close-set ribs and finished it off with long gunwale planks. He set up a mast, and a yard to cross it, and shaped a steering-oar to hold his course. He fenced the whole length of it with woven willow against the seas, and threw down a good ballast of brush. Then Calypso, fair among goddesses, brought cloth for the sail, and he made that well too, and bound the braces and halyards and sheets in place. And at last, with levers, he hauled the raft down to the bright sea.

By the fourth day he had the whole of it finished, and on the fifth Calypso, fair among goddesses, sent him from the island, after she had bathed him and dressed him in sweet-smelling clothes. She put aboard one skin of dark wine and a second, larger one of water, and a bag of provisions besides, and many good things to eat. And she sent a fair, warm wind after him, and great-hearted Odysseus spread his sail to it with joy, and sat by the steering-oar and held his course like a master. Sleep never fell on his eyes; he kept them fixed on the Pleiades, and on Boötes that sets so late, and on the Bear — which men also call the Wain — that wheels forever in its place, watching Orion, and alone takes no part in the baths of Ocean. For Calypso, fair among goddesses, had told him to keep that star on his left hand as he crossed the sea. Seventeen days he sailed the open water, and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains of the Phaeacian land rose up, where it stood nearest to him, lifting like a shield out of the misty sea.

But lord Poseidon, the shaker of the earth, on his way back from the Ethiopians, caught sight of him far off, from the mountains of the Solymi. He saw Odysseus sailing the sea, and a great rage swelled in him, and he shook his head and muttered to his own heart: "So this is it — the gods have changed their minds about Odysseus while I was away among the Ethiopians. He's already close to the Phaeacian shore, where it is his fate to slip the great net of suffering that has him fast. But I think I can still drive him his fill of trouble yet."

With that he gathered the clouds together and seized his trident in both hands and churned the sea, and roused the blasts of every wind that blows, and hid land and water alike in cloud, and night came rushing down out of the sky. The East Wind and the South Wind clashed together, and the hard-blowing West and the North that is born in the clear air rolling a great wave before it. And the knees of Odysseus went slack, and his heart with them, and he groaned to his own great spirit: "What sorrow — what is to become of me now? I'm afraid the goddess told it true, every word, when she said I'd fill my cup of suffering at sea before I ever reached home. Now all of it is coming to pass. Look at the clouds Zeus is wreathing the whole sky in — and the sea churned wild, and the gusts of every wind hurling down at once. There's no escape now; my ruin is certain. Three times blessed, four times blessed, were the Greeks who died back then on the wide plain of Troy, doing the work of the sons of Atreus. I wish I had died there, met my end on the day the Trojans came at me in their thousands, around the dead body of Achilles. I'd have had my funeral rites, and the Greeks would have carried my name down the years. Instead it's a wretched death I'm fated to be taken by."

As the words left him a great wave crashed down from above, terrible, driving hard, and spun the raft around. He was flung far overboard, and the steering-oar tore from his hands, and the fury of the warring winds snapped his mast clean in the middle, and the sail and the yard went flying far out into the sea. The water held him under a long time; he could not fight back up at once against the rush of the great wave, for the clothes Calypso had given him dragged him down. At last he broke the surface and spat out the bitter brine that streamed in rivers from his head. Battered as he was, he did not forget his raft. He lunged through the waves and caught hold of it and pulled himself up into the middle of it, and so he kept clear of death. The great swell carried the raft this way and that on the current, the way the North Wind in autumn drives the thistledown across a field, the tufts clinging together — so the winds bore it back and forth across the sea, now the South Wind tossing it to the North to carry, now the East giving it over to the West to chase.

But Ino saw him — the daughter of Cadmus, Ino of the slim ankles, who is also called Leucothea. She was once a mortal of human speech, but now in the salt depths she holds her share of honor among the gods. She pitied Odysseus as he drifted in his misery, and rose from the water like a sea-gull on the wing, and settled on the raft, and spoke to him. "My poor man — why is Poseidon the earth-shaker so set against you, sowing all this trouble in your path? Yet he will not destroy you, for all his fury. Do as I tell you — you seem to have your wits about you. Strip off those clothes, leave your raft to the winds, and swim with your arms for the Phaeacian shore, where it is your fate to come through. Here — take this veil of mine and stretch it under your chest. It is immortal; you need fear nothing now, no suffering, no drowning. But the moment your hands touch land, untie it and fling it far out into the wine-dark sea, well clear of the shore, and turn your face away." With that the goddess gave him the veil, and dove back down into the heaving sea like a gull, and the dark water closed over her.

But long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus was torn, and groaned to his own great spirit: "No — I'm afraid this is one of the immortals weaving me another trap, telling me to leave my raft. I won't do it, not yet. That land where she says I'll be safe — I saw with my own eyes it's still a long way off. Here's what I'll do, and I think it's best: as long as the timbers hold together, I'll stay aboard and ride out the worst. But the moment the sea smashes the raft to pieces, then I'll swim for it — there's nothing better I can think of than that."

While he was still turning it over in his mind, Poseidon the earth-shaker raised up a great wave, terrible and crushing, towering over him, and brought it down. As a wild gust scatters a dry heap of chaff and flings it every way, so the long timbers flew apart. Odysseus threw himself astride a single beam and rode it like a man on horseback, and stripped off the clothes Calypso had given him, and wound Ino's veil beneath his chest, and plunged headlong into the sea, his arms spread to swim. And lord Poseidon, the shaker of the earth, saw him do it, and shook his head, and muttered to his own heart: "There — now drift in misery across the sea, until you fall in with men whom the gods have favored. Even so, I don't think you'll find your suffering too light." With that he whipped his fine-maned horses on and drove to Aegae, where his glorious palace stands.

But Athena, daughter of Zeus, had other plans. She bound back the paths of all the other winds and ordered them to rest, to fall still and sleep — all but the swift North Wind, which she roused, and she broke the waves down ahead of brilliant Odysseus, so that he might reach the Phaeacians, who love their oars, and slip past death and doom.

For two nights then, and two days, he drifted on the heavy swell, and again and again his heart looked his own death in the face. But when fair-haired Dawn brought on the third day, the wind died and a windless calm came over the sea, and there, as he was lifted high on a great swell and peered ahead with straining eyes, he saw land close by. As welcome as the first sign of life is to children, when their father lies sick, racked with long agony, wasting under some cruel god's hand, and then the gods set him free of the evil — that welcome was the sight of land and trees to Odysseus, and he swam hard for it, longing to set his feet on solid ground. But when he had come within shouting distance of the shore, he heard the boom of the surf against the rocks. Great waves were thundering in against the dry land with a terrible roar, and everything was sheeted in spray. There were no harbors there to hold a ship, no roadstead — only headlands jutting out, and reefs, and cliffs.

And the knees of Odysseus went slack, and his heart with them, and he groaned to his own great spirit: "What now? Zeus has let me see the land I'd given up all hope of, and I've cut my way clear across this gulf — but there's no way out of the gray water, no foothold. Sharp rocks ahead, and the surf roaring all around them, and the cliff rising up sheer and smooth, with deep water hard against it, no place to stand on my two feet and pull free of this ruin. If I try to climb out, a great wave will lift me and dash me against the jagged rock, and my struggle is for nothing. But if I swim on further, looking for a beach that shelves easy, or a quiet harbor, I'm afraid the storm will snatch me up again, groaning, and carry me back out over the teeming sea — or some god will send a great monster up against me from the deep, the kind that famed Amphitrite breeds by the thousand. For I know how the great earth-shaker hates me."

While he was still turning it over in his mind, a great wave carried him in against the rugged shore. There he would have been flayed, his bones broken, had not grey-eyed Athena put it into his heart what to do. He lunged with both hands and caught the rock and clung to it, groaning, until the great wave had passed. So he rode that one out — but then the backwash struck him and flung him far out to sea again. As when an octopus is torn from its hole and the pebbles cling thick to its suckers, so the skin was stripped from his strong hands against the rock, and the great wave closed over him. And there, against all his fate, poor Odysseus would have died, had not grey-eyed Athena given him a clear head. He fought up clear of the surf where it pounded the shore, and swam along outside it, his eyes always on the land, looking for a beach that shelved easy or a harbor out of the sea's reach. And as he swam he came to the mouth of a fair-running river, and that, he saw, was the best place of all — smooth, no rocks, and sheltered from the wind. He felt the river's current running and he prayed to it in his heart:

"Hear me, lord, whoever you are. I come to you as the answer to all my prayers, fleeing the sea and Poseidon's threats. Even the deathless gods honor the man who comes to them lost and wandering, the way I come now to your stream and your knees, after so much suffering. Take pity on me, lord. I am your suppliant, and I claim it."

So he prayed, and the river-god at once held back his current and stilled the waves, and made the water smooth before him, and brought him safe to land at the river's mouth. There at last his knees gave way, and his strong hands, for the sea had broken him utterly. His whole body was swollen, and the sea-water ran streaming from his mouth and nose, and he lay there with no breath in him and no voice, worn out past all enduring. But when at last he caught his breath and the spirit gathered again in his heart, he untied the goddess's veil from his body and let it fall into the seaward-running river, and a great wave bore it back down the current, and Ino caught it in her hands at once. Then he turned from the river, sank down in the reeds, and kissed the grain-giving earth.

And still, in his misery, he groaned to his own great spirit: "What now — what's to become of me, here at the end of everything? If I keep watch by the river through the long, anxious night, the bitter frost and the soaking dew may finish me off, weak as I am, breath barely in me — and a cold wind blows up off a river toward dawn. But if I climb the slope to the shadowy woods and lie down to sleep in the thick brush, even if the cold and the weariness let me be and sweet sleep comes — I'm afraid I'll be left as prey, a meal for the wild beasts."

In the end this seemed the better course. He went up toward the woods and found a thicket on rising ground, in a clearing near the water. There he crept in under two olive trees grown from a single root — one a wild olive, the other a cultivated one. No force of the wet, blustering wind could reach through them, no ray of the blazing sun, no soaking rain, so closely had they grown into each other. Odysseus crept in under them, and at once he raked together a wide bed for himself, for there was a great drift of fallen leaves there, enough to cover two men, or three, in the hard weather of deep winter. Brilliant, long-suffering Odysseus saw it and was glad, and lay down in the middle and heaped the fallen leaves over himself. As a man on a lonely farm, far from any neighbor, will bury a glowing brand in the black ashes to save the seed of fire, so he would not have to go begging a light from somewhere else — so Odysseus buried himself in the leaves. And Athena poured sleep over his eyes, and closed his lids, to release him as quickly as she could from his bone-deep weariness.

[Trans. note: The veil Ino gives him is her krēdemnon — a woman's head-binding worn over the hair and drawn across the face. Older versions render it "scarf" or "veil"; we keep "veil," the closest plain English, but the thing is a headdress, an intimate gift of her own covering, immortal and protecting.]

So long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus slept there, worn down by sleep and toil. But Athena went off to the country and the city of the Phaeacians. These people had once lived in the broad land of Hypereia, hard by the Cyclopes, a lawless and overbearing race who were stronger than they were and forever raiding them. So their king, godlike Nausithous, moved them away and settled them in Scheria, far from all other men who live by their labor. He ringed the city with a wall, built houses and temples for the gods, and parceled out the fields. But by now he had gone down, beaten by his fate, to the house of Hades, and Alcinous ruled in his place, a man whose counsels the gods themselves had taught him. It was to his house that grey-eyed Athena came, turning over in her mind the homecoming of great-hearted Odysseus.

She went straight to the richly worked bedchamber where a girl was sleeping who had the form and face of a goddess — Nausicaa, the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous. Two handmaids, lovely as the Graces, lay one on either side of the door, and the gleaming doors were shut. Athena drifted to the girl's bedside like a breath of wind. She had taken the shape of the daughter of Dymas, a famous seafaring man — a girl Nausicaa's own age, and dear to her heart. In that likeness grey-eyed Athena spoke:

"Nausicaa, how did your mother come to have so careless a daughter? Your bright clothes are lying about, neglected — and your wedding is near, when you'll need fine things to wear yourself and fine things to give the bridal party who walk beside you. This is how a girl earns a good name among people, and how she makes her father and her lady mother proud. So come, let's go and wash at the first light of dawn. I'll go along to help, so the work goes quickly, for you won't be a maiden much longer. Already the best young men of all the Phaeacians, your own people, are courting you. Go at first light and ask your noble father to make ready the mules and the cart, to carry the sashes and the robes and the bright bedding. It's better for you to ride than to go on foot — the washing-pools are a long way from the town."

With that, grey-eyed Athena went away to Olympus, where they say the gods have their seat forever, unshaken. No wind shakes it, no rain ever wets it, no snow comes near; the air spreads cloudless and clear, and a white radiance plays over it. There the blessed gods take their pleasure, all their days. To that place the grey-eyed one went, when she had finished with the girl.

Soon Dawn came to her lovely throne and woke Nausicaa of the fine robes. She marveled at her dream, and went off through the house to tell her father and her mother, and she found the two of them inside. Her mother sat at the hearth with her serving women, spinning yarn dyed with sea-purple. She caught her father at the door, on his way out to join the lords of the Phaeacians at their council, where the noblest men had summoned him. She came up close and said:

"Papa, dear — won't you have them harness me a high cart with good wheels, so I can take our fine clothes down to the river to wash? They're lying soiled. And it's right that you yourself should wear clean things when you sit in council among the leading men. And there are five sons of yours under this roof — two of them married, three still in the flower of youth and unwed, and they always want fresh-washed clothes for the dance. All of this is on my mind to see to."

So she spoke, for she was shy of naming her own ripe marriage to her dear father. But he understood it all, and answered her: "I'll not grudge you the mules, child, nor anything else. Off you go — the men will harness you a high cart with good wheels, fitted with a body to hold it all."

With that he called to the servants, and they obeyed. They wheeled the cart out, smooth-running, and harnessed the mules to it and yoked them in, while the girl carried the bright clothes down from her room and stacked them in the polished cart. Her mother packed a hamper with all kinds of good food to eat, and put in savory things, and filled a goatskin with wine; and as the girl climbed up, she gave her soft olive oil in a golden flask, so she and her maids could rub themselves down after the bath. Then Nausicaa took the whip and the bright reins and cracked them to start the mules. They strained against the harness with a clatter of hooves, carrying the clothes and the girl — not alone, for her handmaids walked along beside her.

When they reached the beautiful stream of the river, where the washing-pools never failed — clear water welling up in plenty to wash the dirtiest clothes — they unyoked the mules from the cart and turned them loose along the eddying river to graze on the honey-sweet grass. They lifted the clothes down from the cart by armfuls, carried them into the dark water, and trod them down in the pits, each girl racing the others at the work. When they had washed them and rinsed every stain away, they spread them out in a row along the seashore, where the surf had washed the shingle cleanest. Then they bathed, and rubbed themselves with the glistening oil, and ate their meal beside the banks of the river, and waited for the clothes to dry in the heat of the sun. And when she and her maids had eaten their fill, they threw off their headscarves and played at ball, and Nausicaa of the white arms led their singing. She moved among them like Artemis the archer ranging the mountains — down the long ridge of Taygetus or Erymanthus, delighting in the wild boar and the swift deer, while the wild nymphs, daughters of Zeus who holds the storm-shield, play at the hunt beside her, and Leto's heart lifts to see her own girl standing a head taller than them all, easy to pick out, lovely as they all are. So this unwed girl outshone her women.

But when she was about to fold the fine clothes, yoke the mules, and turn for home, grey-eyed Athena thought of something else — that Odysseus should wake and see the lovely girl, and she should lead him to the city of the Phaeacians. The princess threw the ball to one of her maids; it missed her and dropped into a deep eddy of the river, and they all cried out, loud and clear. And brilliant Odysseus woke. He sat up, and a question turned in his heart and mind:

"What sorrow — whose country have I come to this time? Are they cruel men, savage, with no sense of right? Or do they welcome strangers, and fear the gods in their hearts? That sounded to me like the high cry of girls — like the nymphs who haunt the steep peaks of the mountains, and the springs of rivers, and the grassy water-meadows. Or am I somewhere near people who speak as I do? Let me go and see for myself."

With that, brilliant Odysseus crept out from under the bushes, and with his strong hand he broke off a leafy branch from the thick wood, to hold across his body and cover his nakedness. And out he came, like a lion bred in the hills, sure of its strength, that goes out through wind and rain with its eyes ablaze, and falls on the cattle and the sheep, or hunts the wild deer — its belly drives it to break even into a close-fenced steading after the flock. So Odysseus, in his hard need, made ready to wade in among the girls with their lovely hair, naked as he was. He came toward them, caked with brine, a terrible sight, and they scattered in fear, this way and that, along the jutting spits of the shore. Only the daughter of Alcinous held her ground, for Athena put courage in her heart and took the fear from her limbs. She stood and faced him.
